item.title: Theoretical study of high-order harmonic generation in solids based on deep-learning methods
item.description: arXiv:2610.35991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-order harmonic generation (HHG) in solids provides a compact and coherent EUV radiation, which has attracted considerable attention. Many theoretical methods for laser-crystal interactions are developed. However, an approach to treat large-scale amorphous systems with ab-initio accuracy is still lacking because of the enormous computational cost. Here, we incorporate molecular dynamics and tight-binding electron Hamiltonians based on deep-learning methods to solve the problem efficiently. Its accuracy is validated by comparing the HHG spectra of monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) with those obtained using existing methods. Then we use it to study the temperature-dependent HHG in bulk Si. We uncover a distinct harmonic-order-dependent thermal response: low-order harmonics are enhanced with increasing temperature, whereas high-order harmonics are suppressed. The former is caused by the modification of the inter-site hopping in the system, while the latter is mainly influenced by the structural disorder induced by the thermal effects, in agreement with experimental observations. This work establishes a scalable computational strategy for investigating HHG in solids and provides new insights into the interplay between lattice fluctuations and ultrafast electron dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Wen-Feng Huang, Jia-Qi Liu, Xue-Bin Bian

item.title: Parameter-Decoupled Superresolution with Airy-Disk-Informed Learning: Application to NGC 4486B
item.description: arXiv:2610.36021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating the separation of two unresolved or nearly unresolved sources from recorded intensity images is difficult when source brightness, mutual coherence, and phase are unknown and the point-spread function (PSF) departs from a Gaussian. We formulate Hermite--Gaussian (HG) projections of one- and two-dimensional Airy amplitudes and prove that ratios of mode probabilities with equal longitudinal parity exactly cancel the brightness, coherence, and phase nuisance parameters under a symmetric two-source model. For a one-dimensional Airy slice we achieve an explicit multi-ratio separation inversion. For the physical two-dimensional circular-pupil PSF we obtain exact finite-pupil overlap integrals and locally invertible separation responses. Motivated by these analytical invariants, we examine Airy-informed convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on synthetic Airy images with known separations. At 150,000 training images, the approximate mean absolute errors are 0.018 in plotted separation units, 10 times better comparing to 0.18 for non-Airy Gaussian PSF approximation. Applied to an archival Hubble Space Telescope image of the double nucleus of NGC 4486B, the Airy-informed CNN gives estimates of approximately 9.6--12.0 pc for training sets of 100,000--150,000 images, broadly consistent with the historical approximately 12 pc value. We distinguish exact optical-mode nuisance cancellation from empirical robustness of an image-only learned estimator and identify the limits imposed by PSF mismatch and extended galaxy structure.
item.dc:creator: James Qu, Isabella L. Lee, Gang Zhang, Abdelali Sajia, Yashashree Jadhav, Xiao-Feng Qian

item.title: Ultrafast light-electron modulation for free-electron quantum optics: fundamentals and applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.36182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coherent optical modulation of free-electron wavepackets offers a route to ultrafast beam steering, energy exchange, temporal compression, and quantum-state shaping. Recent advances in photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (PINEM), ultrafast Kapitza-Dirac effect (KDE) and dielectric laser acceleration (DLA) have demonstrated strong light-electron coupling, but longitudinal energy modulation, transverse momentum transfer, and wavepacket-dependent diffraction are still commonly described with separate models. Here, we develop a unified Light-Electron Modulation (LEM) framework that treats optical near fields as programmable phase modulators for free-electron wavepackets. Within this framework, we identify longitudinal and transverse modulation channels, analogous to electro-optic phase modulation and acousto-optic diffraction of light, respectively, and show how their operation depends on wavepacket extent, recoil, phase matching, and optical-field geometry. This formulation organizes PINEM, Raman-Nath and Bragg diffraction, DLA-like acceleration, and anomalous PINEM as limiting regimes of a common modulation picture. The resulting framework provides design principles for free-electron modulators that can control energy spectra, temporal density, transverse wavefronts, and electron-photon quantum interfaces, establishing LEM as a device-level platform for programmable femtosecond-to-attosecond matter-wave control.
item.dc:creator: Zirui Zhao, Ruoyu Chen, Changying Li, Yongcheng Ding, Zhaopin Chen, Xinbing Song, Shuaishuai Sun, Ye Tian, Kangpeng Wang, Yiming Pan

item.title: Multi-day single-cell magnetic imaging of living cancer cells using Quantum Cell Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2610.36359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Live-cell imaging of cellular and tissue samples relies predominantly on optical modalities, such as fluorescence, confocal, and multiphoton microscopy, in which cellular information is encoded in emitted photons. Photons scatter and attenuate in biological samples, restricting depth resolution, while the excitation light required to produce them induces photodamage that perturbs the very biology under observation. Magnetic fields, by contrast, traverse biological samples without attenuation at cellular length scales, but the imaging modality that extracts the encoded information, magnetic resonance imaging, cannot resolve individual cells. Here we present Quantum Cell Monitoring (QCM), a widefield nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry platform that encodes single-cell information in stray magnetic fields rather than emitted photons and reads it out at subcellular resolution. Integrated with a specialized live-cell incubator, QCM tracks magnetically labeled living cancer for up to 72 h through their individual magnetic field signatures. It captures single-cell mitosis and morphological remodeling, as well as cell cluster formation, splitting, and migration even within dense regions where brightfield contrast collapses. By shifting the carrier of single-cell information from propagating optical photons to static magnetic stray fields, QCM decouples cell from cellular optical accessibility and auto-fluorescence, enabling sustained live-cell observation in regimes inaccessible to optical microscopy.
item.dc:creator: Andre Pointner, Sarah Belasi, Regine Schneider-Stock, Roland Nagy

item.title: High-Efficiency Graphene Oxide Moir\'e Lenses Enabled by Cyclic Self-Assembly and Laser Nanoprinting
item.description: arXiv:2610.36373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compact optical systems with continuously tunable focal lengths are highly desirable for machine vision, biomedical imaging, and miniaturized cameras. Rotational Moir\'e lenses offer a planar approach to focal-length tuning, but metasurface-based implementations typically require complex nanofabrication processes that complicate large-area production. Here, we present a cyclic, mask-free fabrication strategy that combines layer-by-layer self-assembly of two-dimensional graphene oxide (GO) and poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (PDDA) with femtosecond laser nanoprinting. Repeated GO-PDDA assembly and spatially selective ablation enable atomic-scale thickness control and the construction of precise multilevel phase profiles, reducing phase-quantization errors and improving focusing efficiency. The measured focusing efficiencies of individual GO lenses increase from 22.4% for two phase levels to 54.8% for six levels. Using this six-level modulation strategy, the fabricated GO Moir\'e lens achieves continuous focal-length tuning from approximately 10 to 90 mm. Full-colour imaging with magnifications ranging from 1X to 9X is experimentally demonstrated. These results establish a cyclic, mask-free fabrication strategy for efficient multilevel GO flat optics and demonstrate its potential for compact, reconfigurable imaging.
item.dc:creator: Guiyuan Cao, Xinyuan Du, Han Lin, Baohua Jia, Shibiao Wei

item.title: Optically gated transduction enables silicon electrical readout of mid-infrared light
item.description: arXiv:2610.36475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Silicon is the dominant platform for integrated photonics, yet its wide electronic bandgap of 1.1 eV fundamentally prevents efficient detection of mid-infrared (MIR) photons through direct valence band to conduction band excitation. Existing approaches therefore seek to enhance sub-bandgap absorption or introduce external infrared absorbers. Here we demonstrate a profoundly different detection strategy based on optically gated transduction, in which MIR photons modulate a pre-established excitation state rather than directly generating photocarriers. Our device integrates Nd3+-doped lanthanide nanoparticles with an inverse-designed Al/p-Si metasurface supporting dual resonances that simultaneously enhances optical gating in the near infrared and resonantly couples incident MIR radiation. The MIR illumination redistributes the Nd3+ emission pathways, producing an optical-state change that is converted into an electrical signal through a silicon Schottky junction. The device achieves room-temperature zero-bias detection at 6.8 um with a modulation responsivity of 103 uA/W and resolves combined gate and MIR inputs into three electrically distinguishable current states. Rather than extending silicon absorption into the infrared, this work establishes gated optical transduction as a route for reading MIR optical information on a silicon platform, opening opportunities for integrated infrared sensing, signal processing and programmable photonic systems.
item.dc:creator: Shutao Zhang, Jiaqing Shen, Chongwu Wang, Jiahui Xu, Wei Chen, Qing Yang Steve Wu, Yan Liu, Xie Yuen Gok, Febiana Tjiptoharsono, Xiaogang Liu, Qi Jie Wang, Joel K. W. Yang, Jinfeng Zhu, Zhaogang Dong

item.title: Study of Multilayer TiNx/Ti/TiNx Films Formed In Situ for High-Efficiency Integrated Microheaters
item.description: arXiv:2610.37130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A technology for the in situ formation of a three-layer TiN$_x$/Ti/TiN$_x$ functional material within a single vacuum cycle is presented, together with the results of investigations of its structural and electrophysical properties. The maximum critical power density reached approximately 140 MW/cm$^2$. Under continuous operation at 90% of the critical power, the structures remained operational for 24 h. The characteristics of microbridges without and with a protective SiO$_x$ layer were compared. The presence of the coating modifies the electrothermal operating regime of the structures and enables estimated temperatures of approximately 500-700 degrees Celsius to be reached.
item.dc:creator: Oleg A. Solovyev, Zakhar S. Enbaev, Alexander R. Shevchenko, Aleksander M. Mumlyakov, Pavel A. Berezhnoy, Mikael O. Geodakyan, Mikhail V. Tsvetkov, Michael A. Tarkhov, Igor V. Trofimov

item.title: Channel-Differentiated Topological Charge Flips and Formation of Janus Bound States in the Continuum in Single-Layer Photonic Lattices
item.description: arXiv:2610.37168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The topological charge of a bound state in the continuum (BIC) can flip when the BIC merges with other polarization singularities or, as recently shown, at band flips. Here, using a coupled-mode analysis, we derive an analytical expression for the topological charge of symmetry-protected BICs in one-dimensional single-layer photonic lattices. The expression captures both merging-induced and band-flip-induced charge flips. We find that, during a band flip, the topological charge of the BIC reverses with the formation of lines of circular polarization that cross at the $\Gamma$ point. In vertically symmetric lattices, each charge flip occurs simultaneously in the upward and downward radiation channels. Breaking vertical symmetry makes both kinds of charge flips channel-differentiated, creating a parameter interval in which the BIC carries opposite topological charges in the two channels and forms a Janus BIC. We show that Janus BICs also emerge in experimentally accessible one- and two-dimensional silicon-based photonic lattices. Our results link the topological charge of a BIC directly to the band structure and the channel-resolved radiation amplitudes and establish a basis for channel-selective control of polarization singularities.
item.dc:creator: Sun-Goo Lee, Wook-Jae Lee

item.title: Wavefunction-templated metamaterials
item.description: arXiv:2610.37248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metamaterials, which store, guide and emit waves through their eigenmodes, have enabled the development of devices with unprecedented functionalities. Yet the spatial profiles of conventional metamaterials' eigenmodes are typically determined by their pre-determined structures (Hamiltonians). In this work, we introduce `wavefunction-templated metamaterials', a class of physically realizable metamaterials hosting diverse prescribed, spectrally isolated eigenstates. The resulting Hamiltonian geometries obey a boundary law, with the required nonlocality determined solely by single-contact boundary sites, independent of the state interior or lattice size. The sparse Hamiltonians are then Hermitianized, followed by spectral reshaping to open a protective gap around the target eigenstate. We validate our approach in discrete lattices and acoustic metamaterials. Although demonstrated in acoustics, the principle can be applied to thermal, electrical-circuit and photonic metamaterials.
item.dc:creator: Yutao Chen, Tao Xiao, Jing Li, Aodong Li, Biye Xie

item.title: Rubidium-Referenced Frequency-Doubled Pockels Laser with High-Speed Electro-Optic Tuning
item.description: arXiv:2610.37279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Narrow-linewidth lasers with rapid frequency control are essential for atomic physics and quantum technologies, yet combining these capabilities in chip-integrated sources at visible wavelengths remains challenging. Here we demonstrate a hybrid integrated InP/thin-film lithium niobate Pockels laser that emits at 780 nm through intracavity second-harmonic generation and supports gigahertz-bandwidth frequency tuning. A periodically poled lithium niobate waveguide is embedded in a laser cavity terminated by an extended distributed Bragg reflector, which provides electro-optically tunable feedback only at the 1560 nm fundamental wavelength. This design yields a singly resonant cavity that enhances frequency conversion while allowing the second-harmonic output to follow rapid tuning without resonance alignment. The laser achieves intrinsic linewidths of 2.7 kHz at 1560 nm and 9.0 kHz at 780 nm, with electro-optic tuning bandwidths beyond 1 GHz at both wavelengths. A mode-hop-free tuning range of 6.48 GHz at 780 nm enables direct spectroscopy of the rubidium D2 transition. Locking the second-harmonic output to this transition reduces the standard deviation of its frequency fluctuations from 135 MHz to 8 MHz and transfers the atomic frequency reference to the fundamental. These results establish integrated frequency-doubled Pockels lasers as compact, rapidly tunable sources that could simplify the optical architectures for future atomic and quantum photonic systems.
item.dc:creator: Xu Chen, Michael Li, Xiaodong Shi, Lin Zhou, Ran Yang, Mengyao Zhao, Veerendra Dhyani, Sakthi Sanjeev Mohanraj, Guangxing Wu, Hao Hao, Xia Yu, Di Zhu

item.title: Surface-Illuminated Interdigitated Ge-on-Si Avalanche Photodiode With Separated Ge Absorption, Si Multiplication, and Lateral Field Engineering
item.description: arXiv:2610.37593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work presents a surface-illuminated lateral Ge-on-Si interdigitated separate-absorption-charge-multiplication (SACM) avalanche photodiode for 1550-nm detection. The intrinsic-region spacing, P$^-$ charge-control width, and finger geometry are engineered to suppress high-field penetration toward the Ge/Si heterointerface and localize avalanche multiplication in Si. Simulations show that wider charge-control or intrinsic regions reduce fixed-bias dark current and shift avalanche onset to higher reverse bias. Among the tested structures, the intrinsic-region spacing/P$^-$ charge-control width of 0.5/0.15 $\mu$m achieved a peak responsivity of 11.81 A/W at 1550 nm. At a -20 V applied voltage, it exhibited a multiplication gain of 3.796, a 3-dB bandwidth of 7.13 GHz, and a matched-bias gain-bandwidth product of 27.07 GHz. Optical-power-dependent measurements also show avalanche-gain compression consistent with space-charge screening. These results demonstrate effective lateral-field engineering for high-speed, surface-illuminated Ge-on-Si APDs.
item.dc:creator: Mason Clewis, Kuang-Yun Tu, Ching-Yu Hsu, Zingway Pei

item.title: Catastrophes in Reconnections of Optical Vortex Rings
item.description: arXiv:2610.37615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A small change in parameters leads to a small change in the outcomes, in most cases. For instance, an optical vortex ring, created in the superposition of two laser beams, can slightly shrink if the phase changes minutely. However, dynamical systems can also experience significant changes due to small perturbations in parameters; the vortex rings can reconnect, nucleate or collapse into a point. Parameters that cause such striking outcomes are at the focal point of catastrophe theory - a branch of bifurcation theory that studies degenerate critical points of a potential function. We present theoretical study of topological configurations of optical vortex rings in elliptic Gaussian beams, which change dramatically at specific beam parameters. We identify two types of catastrophes, cusp and butterfly, near which very small changes of elliptic deformations lead to complex topological transformations of vortex rings.
item.dc:creator: Zhamila Kulchukova, Albert Ferrando, Anton S. Desyatnikov

item.title: Tunable turning point of the frequency--temperature response in suspended bilayer SiN_x/Al nanofilms
item.description: arXiv:2610.35977v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Non-invasive thermometry is highly desirable in cryogenic experiments to avoid the self-heating inherent in conventional sensors. In previous work, temperature was probed via the vibrational eigenfrequency of a suspended single-layer SiNx nanofilm. However, the turning point of the frequency-temperature curve limited the usable measurement range. Moreover, the slow thermal response confined measurements to a stepwise protocol with only discrete temperature points. Here, we show that these limitations can be overcome with a suspended bilayer SiNx/Al nanofilm, whose temperature-dependent vibrational eigenfrequency provides a monotonic, continuous, and repeatable temperature readout. The frequency-temperature dependence is governed by the mismatch between the effective coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE) of the bilayer and the substrate, which makes the turning point tunable through the thickness ratio of the two layers. Over the 90 K to 300 K range, we characterize three bilayer nanofilms with different Al layer thicknesses and show how the turning point shifts with the thickness of the Al layer. For the sample with 72 nm Al, the turning point is pushed beyond 300 K, yielding a monotonic negative temperature coefficient over the entire 90 K to 300 K range. Combining a thin Al layer on the SiNx film with improved thermal anchoring of the chip shortens the thermal response to below 1 s, enabling continuous frequency tracking at a ramp rate of 3 K/min. We also demonstrate that the nanofilm with a 72 nm Al layer achieves a repeatability better than 150 mK above 175 K, and the frequency resolution of 1 Hz corresponds to a temperature resolution of ~5 mK.
item.dc:creator: Yanli Shi, Hui Wu, Guangyu Li, Zhuo Miao, Luyao Zhu, Chen Zheng, Weidong Zheng, Qun Cao, Zhe He, Zheng Cui

item.title: Quantum circuit simulation with high-order optical tensor processing
item.description: arXiv:2610.36172v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Classical simulation is essential for developing and testing quantum circuits, but the exponential growth of Hilbert space challenges conventional digital processors. Here, we introduce a classical optical quantum simulation architecture that treats gates and batches of input states as independent tensor dimensions rather than separate simulation instances, while mapping eligible tensor network contractions onto the same processor. Using co-designed multidimensional encoding and readout across spatial and wavelength degrees of freedom, we experimentally realize high-order tensor-matrix multiplication in a single propagation and process all computational-basis inputs for each 4-qubit gate. Using a physics-based optical propagation model, we further numerically evaluate the architecture for the Deutsch algorithm and for the tensor network of all 128 target instances of a 7-qubit Grover algorithm. These results establish a unified framework for gate-state batch and tensor network simulation, providing a route to exploit optical concurrency across quantum simulation tasks.
item.dc:creator: Yufeng Zhang, Xuhan Guo, Zixuan Ning, Zhiliang Yuan, Yikai Su, Kaizhi Wang, Sergei Turitsyn, Zhipei Sun

item.title: Generation of quantum light with tunable Wigner negativity with a semiconductor quantum dot
item.description: arXiv:2610.36233v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wigner-negative states of light are key resources for quantum advantage in continuous-variable optical quantum computing. They can be produced probabilistically via frequency conversion and photon detection, or deterministically by exploiting the single-photon nonlinearity of a quantum emitter. Here, we generate such Wigner-negative states of light with a tunable negativity using a single semiconductor quantum dot in a cavity. Optical coherent control of the quantum-dot transition allows to generate a quantum superposition of zero and one photon. The generated quantum states are characterized point-by-point in the phase space through homodyne measurement. The emergence of Wigner-function negativity is observed as the excitation power is increased. After correcting for collection and propagation losses, we obtain fidelities to the ideal state and quantum purities above 95%, together with near-optimal quadrature squeezing. The ability to generate a wide variety of Wigner-negative states with mature semiconductor technology opens promising opportunities for continuous-variable optical quantum technologies.
item.dc:creator: Hubert Lam, Petr Steindl, Yann Portella, Kiarn T. Laverick, Kian Hwee Lim, Juan R. Alvarez, Aristide Lemaitre, Maria Maffei, Alexia Auffeves, Dario A. Fioretto, Pascale Senellart

item.title: Spectral Oscillations and Temporal Meandering of Dissipative Solitons in a Moving Intracavity Phase Potential
item.description: arXiv:2610.36504v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dissipative solitons (DSs) provide a prototypical platform for studying nonequilibrium dynamics governed by the interplay between nonlinearity, dissipation, and external driving. In particular, subjected to external potentials, DSs exhibit a rich variety of nonlinear dynamical behaviors. This work investigates DS dynamics in a moving intracavity potential generated by phase modulation whose frequency is detuned from an integer multiple of the cavity repetition rate. Modulation detuning introduces a timescale mismatch between the DS and the moving potential, leading to two distinct dynamical regimes. At large detuning, the DS cannot continuously track the moving potential and exhibits persistent spectral oscillations and temporal meandering, whereas at sufficiently small detuning it enters a synchronized locking state. Furthermore, both the oscillation period and amplitude can be tuned via the modulation detuning and modulation depth. These results reveal how asynchronous driving reshapes DS dynamics and establish a route for controlling their dynamical response in nonlinear optical cavities.
item.dc:creator: Heng Dong, Xiankun Yao, Wen-Li Yang

item.title: Bright Solitons in Non-Hermitian systems: Exploring the interplay of $\mathcal{PT}$ Symmetry and Wadati Structure
item.description: arXiv:2610.36706v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this study, we revisit the subject of optical solitons in non-Hermitian potentials. For the underlying model of the focusing nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation with a complex localized potential, we offer a classification of such models into four canonical cases. These correspond to (a) $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric Wadati potentials, (b) $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric non-Wadati potentials, (c) Non-$\mathcal{PT}$ but Wadati potentials, and (d) complex potentials with neither $\mathcal{PT}$ nor Wadati symmetries. We study the existence and stability of optical solitons across prototypical model variations spanning all four relevant quadrants. We complement such an investigation with a low-dimensional effective description based on a non-conservative variational approximation method. The variational framework is assessed in terms of its ability to represent the structural properties and bifurcations of solutions. {Our results suggest that continuous families of bright solitons persist across sectors (a)--(c). For non-$\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric potentials, small departures from the Wadati limit, corresponding to sector (d), suggest the loss of continuous families of bright-solitons including, more specifically, the possibility of the generic absence of single-humped localized states. The corresponding variational analysis is broadly consistent with these observations. We also highlight the usefulness and limitations for such variational approaches in describing bright solitons in the presence of non-Hermitian potentials.
item.dc:creator: Sathyanarayanan Chandramouli, Ricardo Carretero-Gonz\'alez, Dimitrios J. Frantzeskakis, Panayotis G. Kevrekidis

item.title: Adaptive Information Mining: Approaching the Quantum Limit of Super-Resolution Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2610.37491v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The "Rayleigh limit" is not an intrinsic property of light, but a consequence of sub-optimal measurement of collected photons by the imaging instrument. To overcome this limitation, we present Adaptive Information Mining, a framework that achieves super-resolution by using sequentially refined measurements for incoming photons. Our approach employs a reconfigurable imaging system that dynamically reshapes the instrument measurement responses to maximize the Fisher information and guide scene estimation toward the fundamental quantum limit, even in deep sub-Rayleigh regimes. We demonstrate that this approach achieves an estimation error 2-5 times closer to the fundamental quantum limit than traditional direct imaging when imaging point sources, without requiring any prior knowledge of their positions and brightnesses. Importantly, we demonstrate that AIM can be extended to fully blind multi-parameter estimation in scenarios involving an unknown number of sources or turbulence-induced wavefront distortions. Our approach addresses the limitations of conventional fixed imaging, offering a practical path toward quantum-limited super-resolution imaging.
item.dc:creator: Seungman Choi, Peter Menart, Andrew Schramka, Zubin Jacob

item.title: Optimal quantum discrimination at Liouvillian exceptional points
item.description: arXiv:2610.37660v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Central to non-Hermitian sensing is the question of whether exceptional points (EPs) can make weak perturbations easier to detect. We show that despite enhanced spectral response, in finite-dimensional Lindblad systems with a unique stationary state and a nonzero relaxation gap, EPs offer no fundamental advantage in how the observation time required for reliable detection of a weak perturbation scales with the perturbation strength. We nevertheless demonstrate that by selectively choosing perturbations that enhance the quantum Fisher information rate, EPs can shorten the observation time needed to reach a predefined detection accuracy relative to a comparable non-EP reference at the same decay rate. As an illustration, we show using an optomechanical model at an EP that we can detect a weak force through the cavity output at the same reliability in less time than a non-EP reference. Our results establish fundamental limits on perturbation detection at EPs and can guide the design of faster non-Hermitian sensors based on optomechanical resonators, superconducting qubits, and trapped ions.
item.dc:creator: Aritra Ghosh, M. Bhattacharya

item.title: Quantum structured light: Non-classical spin texture of twisted single-photon pulses
item.description: arXiv:2102.13248v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Classical structured light with controlled polarization and orbital angular momentum (OAM) of electromagnetic waves has varied applications in optical trapping, bio-sensing, optical communications and quantum simulations. The classical electromagnetic theory of such structured light beams and pulses have advanced significantly over the last two decades. However, a framework for the quantum density of spin and OAM for single-photons remains elusive. Here, we develop a theoretical framework and put forth the concept of quantum structured light for space-time wavepackets at the single-photon level. Our work marks a paradigm shift beyond scalar-field theory as well as the paraxial approximation and can be utilized to study the quantum properties of the spin and OAM of all classes of twisted quantum light pulses. We capture the uncertainty in full three-dimensional (3D) projections of vector spin demonstrating their quantum behavior beyond the conventional concept of classical polarization. Even in laser beams with high OAM along the propagation direction, we predict the existence of large OAM quantum fluctuations in the transverse plane which can be verified experimentally. We show that the spin density generates modulated helical texture beyond the paraxial limit and exhibits distinct statistics for Fock-state vs. coherent-state twisted pulses. We introduce the quantum correlator of photon spin density to characterize the nonlocal spin noise providing a rigorous parallel with fermionic spin noise operators. Our work paves the way for quantum spin-OAM physics in twisted single photon pulses and also opens explorations for new phases of light with long-range spin order.
item.dc:creator: Li-Ping Yang, Zubin Jacob

item.title: Trivial topology-entailed states at interfaces between identical topological phases
item.description: arXiv:2202.03252v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Topological edge states arise at boundaries between bulk phases with distinct topological invariants and are characterized by robust, often chiral transport. When two domains sharing identical bulk topology are brought into contact, their counterpropagating edge modes are generally expected to hybridize and cancel each other out in the process. Here, we show that this cancellation can be lifted by trivial parameter variations at the interface, giving rise to a distinct class of gap-localized inter-face modes, which we term trivial topology-entailed (TTE) states. Using anomalous Floquet photonic lattices as a concrete platform, we experimentally observe the formation of bidirectional TTE states between topologically equivalent domains. In particular, we demonstrate their spectral confinement within bulk gaps, their coherent coupling to conventional chiral edge channels, and their ability to mediate interface-guided transport across composite lattices. Our results establish TTE states as a general interface phenomenon in composite topological systems and provide a unified framework for understanding hybridized boundary modes beyond conventional bulk-boundary correspondence.

Piccioli (Institute for Physics, University of Rostock, University of Trento and CNR-INO BEC center), Mark Kremer (Institute for Physics, University of Rostock), Max Ehrhardt (Institute for Physics, University of Rostock), Lukas J. item.title: Super bound states in the continuum: Classification, direct computation, and geometry in parameter space
item.description: arXiv:2505.00235v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In periodic structures, resonant states near a bound state in the continuum (BIC) have quality ($Q$) factors scaling as $Q\sim 1/\delta^{2\mu}$, where $\delta$ is the wavevector detuning from the BIC. While generic BICs have $\mu=1$, super-BICs with $\mu\geq 2$ give rise to higher-$Q$ resonances over a broad wavevector range, making them attractive for enhancing light-matter interactions. Here, we develop a systematic theoretical and computational framework for studying super-BICs. We first classify them according to $\mu$ and symmetry. We then study their unfolding under structural variations, characterizing the bifurcations of nearby generic BICs and determining the minimum number $n$ of additional tunable structural parameters required to recover a super-BIC of the same class. We devise a direct computational method for locating super-BICs together with their associated structural parameters and efficiently tracing their families. Finally, we investigate the local geometry of the BIC set in the product space of structural parameters and the Brillouin zone. This geometric framework provides a unified interpretation of the unfolding of super-BICs and offers a new understanding of BIC merging and splitting phenomena. Our results establish a theoretical and computational foundation for the systematic study of super-BICs, with potential applications in resonant optics and photonic device design.
item.dc:creator: Nan Zhang, Ya Yan Lu

item.title: Non-Hermitian curved space via inverted wave equation
item.description: arXiv:2602.10937v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Directly determining graded materials from prescribed wave amplitude and phase is an inverse-design method developed following transformation optics (TO), which enables reflectionless propagation for an incidence wave. However, exiting formulations of this inverted method yields Hermitian media and are thus not applicable to non-Hermitian (NH) photonics. In this Letter, we extend this method to NH media, thereby offering more freedom for manipulating waves of no reflection. Our picture of curved-space powered with spatially distributed gain and loss, is exemplified by three types: amplitude control, phase conversion, and direction shunting. These examples showcase precise wave manipulation in a surprisingly simple manner, which is implementable in photonic platform using similar techniques employed in TO.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Photonics and Nanostructures - Fundamentals and Applications (2026)
item.dc:creator: C. Zhang, M. Ikram, Y. Liu, H. Lin, B. Zhou

item.title: Hologram generation using attention for Fraunhofer diffraction
item.description: arXiv:2602.17624v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Controlling optical wavefronts in the strict far-field regime is a fully global inverse problem. Fraunhofer propagation is a single Fourier transform of the aperture, so every modulator pixel couples to every point of the reconstruction and no spatial locality survives for the convolutional priors that dominate learned holography to exploit. Iterative phase retrieval stagnates and trades computation for quality, and camera-in-the-loop methods remain iterative and near-field. Here we show that this global coupling maps naturally onto self-attention, generating a phase-only hologram in a single forward pass of 12 to 24 ms. On hardware, every simulation-trained method collapses to a common floor between 15.8 and 16.1 dB median PSNR set by model-reality mismatch, despite spanning 27.7 to 56.5 dB median PSNR in ideal simulation. Placing the physical optics inside the training loop, which we call self-attention in-the-loop (SAIL), reaches 19.53 dB median PSNR and exceeds the strongest camera-adapted baseline by 0.79 dB on 18 of 18 targets (0.43 dB on 14 of 18 under a more faithful forward model). Most importantly, we show self-attention allows one shared network to serve 18 targets, and as the task complexity increases, the attention mechanism activates. These results establish self-attention as a scalable framework for far-field holography, and attention-based modeling as a general approach to inverse problems governed by long-range interactions in wave physics.
item.dc:creator: Dilawer Singh, Antoni J. Wojcik, Timothy D. Wilkinson

item.title: Fundamental Limit for One versus Two Point Sources Detection using Direct Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2606.00968v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the task of distinguishing between a single weak incoherent optical point source and two weak incoherent optical point sources located symmetrically about the first source. $\theta$ is the separation between the two point sources scaled to the Point Spread Function (PSF) width in the image plane. Using an ideal focal plane array of intensity detectors (ideal direct imaging), we quantify the performance using the Bhattacharyya distance and find the scaling of its leading order term in terms of $\theta$ in the sub-Rayleigh regime. A suite of previous analyses of this problem lacked a comprehensive analysis for when the amplitude spread function (ASF) of the imaging system has zeros and reported a scaling that we find to be incorrect. We complete this analysis by explicitly calculating the leading order term of the Bhattacharyya distance for ideal direct imaging with any ASF, for small $\theta$ and show the difference in scaling based on the presence or absence of zeros in the ASF. This is similar to the ASF dependent performance in the task of estimating the separation between the two point sources and the task of detecting a change to an object. We then apply our results to the specific example of a Gaussian and a Sinc ASF and show good agreement with numerical calculations. Our results allow the accurate comparison of other measurement schemes with ideal direct imaging, and to the quantum limit.
item.dc:creator: Parth Hemant Darekar, Amit Kumar Jha, Michael R. Grace, Aqil Sajjad, Saikat Guha

item.title: Real-Space Double Crossing Reveals Symmetry-Driven Dispersion Back-Bending of Surface Phonon Polaritons on {\alpha}-Quartz
item.description: arXiv:2606.11239v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Surface phonon polaritons (SPhPs) in anisotropic crystals exhibit direction-dependent propagation and dispersion, yet how their dispersion back-bending manifests in real space has not been quantitatively resolved. Here, using nano-Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy based on scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy, we image SPhP fringes on an $\alpha$-quartz surface for propagation parallel and perpendicular to the optic axis. Near 1160 cm$^{-1}$, the fringe periods for the two directions cross twice, providing a real-space signature of back-bending. Spatial Fourier analysis attributes the dominant fringe to edge-launched SPhPs and enables reconstruction of the intrinsic dispersion. Inverse Fourier analysis further visualizes the spatial attenuation and continuous evolution of the fringe wavelength near the resonance. The reconstructed dispersions reveal that the polarization-selective E-mode phonon produces direction-dependent back-bending and, through its damping, reduces the visibility of the back-bending branch. These results establish how symmetry-controlled dispersion manifests in real-space surface polariton propagation on a bulk anisotropic crystal.
item.dc:creator: Ryoga Odawara, Kotaro Shirahata, Aozora Ohi, Shun Hashiyada, Yukio Kawano

item.title: Super-resolution technique enabled by higher-order Bessel beams in nanoscale optical structures
item.description: arXiv:2607.17458v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In conventional optical microscopy, accessing subwavelength information is classically constrained by the Abbe diffraction limit which remains a significant challenge in nanophotonics. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a scheme that generates a tightly confined near-field focal spot under non-diffracting Bessel beam illumination, employing a series of high refractive-index nanoscale structures. Furthermore, the utilization of higher-order Bessel beams enables additional resolution enhancement beyond the diffraction limit. Our results demonstrate that the pyramidal nanostructure can generate a highly localized near-field confinement with a characteristic width of 10 nm, enabling subwavelength optical intensity localization. To elucidate the factors governing the localization behaviour, we systematically investigate the influence of different geometrical parameters related to the incident Bessel beam on the near field localization and shows that these factors critically determine the stability and spatial profile of the focal spot. These findings highlight the potential of the proposed approach for various applications in super-resolution techniques and quantum technology.
item.dc:creator: Apoorva D, M Ummal Momeen

item.title: Inverse-Designed High-Q and Small-Mode-Volume Silicon Nitride Photonic Crystal Cavities for Second- and Third-Harmonic Generation
item.description: arXiv:2608.13261v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: SiN photonic crystal (PhC) cavities are promising platforms for nonlinear and quantum photonics because of their wide transparency window, CMOS compatibility, and negligible two-photon absorption. However, realizing high-Q/V cavities remains challenging because of the relatively low refractive index of SiN. Here, we employ inverse design to optimize a two-dimensional SiN PhC cavity and experimentally demonstrate a quality factor of approximately 80,000, the highest reported for a near-stoichiometric SiN 2D PhC cavity. Furthermore, both second- and third-harmonic generation are observed from the same cavity, providing experimental evidence of strong optical confinement and large Q/V. Our results establish inverse-designed SiN PhC cavities as a promising platform for nonlinear photonics and future heterogeneous integrated photonic devices.
item.dc:creator: M. Takiguchi, P. Heidt, X. Z. Lim, J. Z\"ollner, S. Yanagimoto, K. Nakayama, T. Aihara, M. Ono, H. Sumikura, M. Notomi

item.title: Topological Leading Angular Structure around Bound States in the Continuum
item.description: arXiv:2609.29074v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that the angular structure of the leading radiation around a bound state in the continuum (BIC) directly encodes its topology. This angular information can be determined from the BIC itself and used to design prescribed topological polarization textures. As examples, we identify BICs carrying high topological charges $q=4$ and $q=-5$ in $C_{6v}$ photonic crystal slabs, addressing the question of whether high-charge BICs exist and how they can be systematically realized. We further show that zeros of the leading radiation can drive both topological transitions and the bifurcation of new BIC families. These findings may enable new approaches to polarization engineering in structured light and resonant photonics.
item.dc:creator: Nan Zhang, Ya Yan Lu

item.title: Inverse Design of Integrated Photonic Components for Visible-Light Applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.11453v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) operating in the visible spectral range are crucial for quantum technologies, optical sensing, and nonlinear optics applications. However, their development is hampered by limited integration density and operational bandwidth, linked to low refractive index contrast and restricted parameter space in intuition-based PIC design. We address these bottlenecks with an adjoint-based, fabrication-aware inverse design workflow tailored for visible-spectrum photonics. By expanding the capabilities of FDTDX, an open-source, GPU-accelerated FDTD solver, we provide a versatile memory and runtime efficient inverse design platform. Demonstrating this approach on a silicon nitride (Si3N4) platform, we design, fabricate, and experimentally validate ultra-compact, broadband components for light routing, multiplexing, and polarization control. This work provides a scalable framework for high-density, high-performance visible-light PICs.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Stockinger, Marko \v{S}imi\'c, John O. Adeniran, Natale G. Pruiti, Marc Sorel, Peter Banzer

item.title: Multiport photonic routing with a single cavity-based electro-optic phase shifter per port
item.description: arXiv:2610.31757v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Programmable photonic meshes can perform general linear transformations, but universal transformations on $N$ modes require $O(N^2)$ programmable phase shifters, which cannot simultaneously achieve low drive voltage, gigahertz speed, zero static power, lossless modulation, and a compact footprint. Signal routing does not require universal transformations, which allows considerable circuit simplifications. We present a compact reflective circuit architecture that connects all input-output pairs across $N$ modes in $N$ steps using only $O(N)$ programmable phase shifters. The circuit comprises a single passive $N\times N$ interferometer and a single column of programmable reflective phase shifters. We demonstrate the architecture by implementing a $3\times 3$ router in x-cut thin-film lithium niobate with a passive multimode interferometer and phase shifters based on single-sided photonic-crystal nanobeam cavities. Our programmable devices exhibit a $1.92$ GHz/V resonance tuning efficiency via the Pockels effect, a footprint of $100\,\mu\mathrm{m}^2$, sub-5-V drive voltage, and a 6.2 GHz electro-optic bandwidth. Through voltage-space characterization and physical modeling, we identify routing states with extinction ratios exceeding 11 dB at each output and demonstrate sequential routing at an equipment-limited speed of 10 MHz. Our results establish cavity-enhanced Pockels switching as a routing layer for classical and quantum computing interconnects across visible and near-infrared wavelengths.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Buzzi, Bjarke A. Frederiksen, Dashiell L. P. Vitullo, Mikkel Heuck, Dirk R. Englund

item.title: Video-rate quantitative phase and polarimetric imaging (QP2I) for label-free imaging of contracting muscle cells
item.description: arXiv:2610.32756v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) has become a standard approach for label-free microscopy of transparent specimens, mapping the optical path length. However, the isotropic phase is blind to the molecular order underlying optical anisotropy. Implementations that also add quantitative contrast to birefringence rely on multi-frame illumination or polarization-state scanning, or on dedicated interferometric hardware and thus trade away acquisition speed or the simplicity of a standard microscope. We present Quantitative Phase and Polarimetric Imaging (QPPI), a computational imaging framework that converts a standard differential interference contrast (DIC) microscope with a polarization camera into a single-shot, video-rate, dual-contrast imaging system. We developed a new globally regularized phase reconstruction that eliminates artifacts of prior DIC-to-QPI approaches, providing quantitative phase information, and used per-pixel Stokes-based reconstruction to obtain quantitative anisotropic retardance. We validate the approach across simulations, static reference targets, fixed muscle tissue and living dynamically moving cells. QPPI enables all-optical and label-free studies of contractile dynamics in live cardiomyocytes. It provides both structural and functional readouts at sufficient frame rates to resolve fast cardiomyocyte contractions. Conventional fluorescent labels bleach over time, perturb physiology, and preclude long-term monitoring. Instead, QPPI enables long-term, label-free interrogation of dynamic cellular processes at quantitative contrast and provides structural readouts similar to those provided by established fluorescent labels, such as frame-by-frame sarcomere length. It also offers previously inaccessible measurements, like quantitative analysis of retardance changes during muscle contraction, which provides a direct optical signature of muscle photoelasticity.
item.dc:creator: Lucas Kreiss Roohian, Nachiket Pathak, David Ripp, Mitchell Harling, Nils M. Kronenberg, Marcel Schubert, Malte C. Gather

item.title: Scaling the Wavelength to Optimize Ultrafast Laser Processing of Bandgap Materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.32924v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The spectral characteristics of ultrashort laser pulses offer unique possibilities to control interactions in space and time as well as the subsequent material responses. In particular, selecting the wavelength predefines the fundamental mechanisms governing laser-matter interaction, and thus, how energy is deposited. This Chapter provides an overview on how the essential physical effects in ultrafast laser-matter interaction scale with the wavelength, and the consequences for bandgap material processing applications. First, we recall the main spectral properties of bandgap materials and discuss the important question of the expected processing resolutions depending on wavelength. Then, recent studies on the impact of the wavelength in ultrafast laser-dielectric interaction are presented. Finally, we present how the latest developments in infrared ultrafast laser sources can be advantageously utilized to internally process narrow-gap materials despite challenges related to increased nonlinearities.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Scaling of Laser Processing - Making Light Matter, edited by J. Bonse and A. F. Lasagni, 2026, Springer Nature Switzerland AG
item.dc:creator: Maxime Chambonneau, Mario Garcia-Lechuga, David Grojo, Stefan Nolte

item.title: Integrated electro-optic attention nonlinearities for transformers
item.description: arXiv:2604.09512v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transformers achieve state-of-the-art performance in language processing and computer vision. Their computation increasingly depends on hardware that can keep pace not only with large matrix multiplications, but also with nonlinear operations like Softmax within the core attention mechanism. On digital accelerators, Softmax accounts for only a small fraction of total operations, yet it can disproportionately impact overall inference latency. Here, we use thin-film lithium niobate Mach-Zehnder modulators (MZM) as analog computing elements for low-latency Transformer attention. Our high-speed nonlinearities based on the intrinsic sinusoidal MZM response achieve performance close to digital baselines in Vision Transformers and GPT-2, even under 4-bit input and output quantization. We experimentally characterize the electro-optic response at symbol rates up to 10 GBaud and assess model robustness under corresponding noise conditions. Accounting for the full signal chain, our analysis indicates more than an order of magnitude lower latency relative to previous custom electronic and photonic Softmax implementations. These results establish analog electro-optic devices as nonlinear function units well suited for integration into emerging co-packaged electronic-photonic hardware, offering a path toward high-speed Transformer inference.
item.dc:creator: Luis Mickeler, Kai Lion, Alfonso Nardi, Jost Kellner, Pierre Didier, Bhavin J. Shastri, Niao He, Rachel Grange

item.title: Emergent energy scales in magnonic systems with relative motion
item.description: arXiv:2606.29316v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Relative motion between interacting systems can generate emergent energy scales that are absent in isolated systems. While uniform motion can be eliminated by a Galilean transformation, relative motion between interacting systems generally cannot. By coupling to an excitation's spatial structure, relative motion generates a Doppler frequency determined by its wavevector and the relative velocity, providing a mechanism for driving nonequilibrium phenomena. In this tutorial, we illustrate these ideas using magnonic systems as a concrete platform. We first discuss motion-induced magnon transport between relatively moving ferromagnets, in which the Doppler frequency serves as an effective nonequilibrium bias in the perturbative regime. This mechanism produces magnon currents even without conventional driving forces such as temperature gradients or chemical potential differences. We then introduce motion-induced parametric instabilities. When the emergent scale becomes sufficiently large to resonantly create magnon pairs, the perturbative description breaks down, and the magnonic vacuum becomes unstable. This instability occurs above a critical velocity threshold and leads to spontaneous magnon-pair creation. Connections to related phenomena, including quantum friction, Cherenkov emission, and Zel'dovich superradiance, are also highlighted. The concept of an emergent energy scale provides a unifying framework for understanding transport phenomena and instabilities in quantum systems with relative motion.
item.dc:creator: Daigo Oue

item.title: The Natural Formulation of Cubic-Phase Dynamics in the Linear Potential
item.description: arXiv:2607.25627v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A quantum wave packet in a linear potential, i.e. a constant force such as gravity, accumulates a cubic-in-time phase, universal across Schr\"odinger-type platforms. The natural formulation of the cubic phase dynamics follows from their canonical realization, the Airy eigenstates. The eigenforce, the potential gradient for which the Airy profile is stationary and hence the intrinsic force behind its known self-acceleration absent any applied force, derives from the eigenvalue problem and characterizes the state uniquely up to a rigid translation. Alongside the applied force, it underlies the analytically closed form of these dynamics, comprising three known contributions, intrinsic, force-induced, and a cross term. The force-induced one alone is shape-independent, whereas the Airy eigenstate renders the other two non-dispersing. The cubic coefficient factorizes into two Newtonian force balances, vanishing at the stationary eigenstate and at a non-trivial zero where the phase cancels while the packet keeps accelerating. This exposes the eigenforce as an effective antagonist to the applied force, not only in the caustic's self-acceleration but here also within the phase, while leaving the centroid untouched by Ehrenfest's theorem. Spatially uniform within each packet, it escapes direct measurement, accessible only as the relative phase of two colliding packets, each in its own potential. The relative cubic coefficient is symmetry-forbidden for identical packets and activated by preparation asymmetry. Simulated interference of two truncated Airy packets demonstrates the extraction. Spanning ultracold atoms, paraxial optics, and surface-gravity water waves, it provides a platform-independent probe of the cubic phase and, through its force dependence, of the constant force itself.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian L. D. D. Pellner, Georgi Gary Rozenman
